newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Court says EU law on state aid overrides national law.
newsitem.headline: Court says EU law on state aid overrides national law.

text.p: The European Court of Justice left no doubt on Thursday that European Union law on state aid takes precedence over national law.
The European court told national courts to enforce European Commission decisions to recover illegal state aid paid out to industry, even if under national law the time for recovery is past.

The court reached beyond the issue of national statutes of limitation into the issues of liability on the part of the national state, and legal principles of legitimate expectation to ensure the Commission has authority over state aid.
The granting of DM8 million in aid from Germany to Alcan in 1986 was in dispute from the beginning.
Letters crossed between Germany and the Commision and after Germany considered the Commission late to respond, the aid was awarded. Within months of the award, the Commission ruled the aid illegal.

When Germany failed to comply with the Commission's decision to recover the money, the Commission successfully sued Germany before the court of justice for failure to fulfil member state obligations, in 1989.

The German state of Rheinland then tried to recover the money from Alcan, but it was too late, under German law. German law protects aid recipients acting in good faith from having to return monies, if to do so would create "unreasonable disadvantages."
The court said under the reasonableness standard often applied by courts, Alcan should have known state aid is always subject to Commission approval, and without that approval, subject to revocation.

Noting that Community law cannot preclude national legislation which is based on the protection of legitimate expectations and legal certainty, the court said "undertakings to which aid has been granted may not, in principle, entertain a legitimate expectation that aid is lawful unless it has been granted in compliance with Community procedure...and a diligent businessman should normally be able to determine that."
EXCERPTS FROM THE JUDGMENT
(Court translation into English. Original language of the case: German)
"State aid - Application of national law - Limits"
Case C-24/95
Reference from the court by the Bundesverwaltungsgericht for a preliminary ruling in the proceedings between
Land Rheinland-Pfalz
and
Alcan Deutschland Gmbh
in the prescence of the Oberbundesanwalt beim Bundesverwaltungsgericht

on the interpretation of articles 92 and 93(3) of the EC Treaty with regard to the obligation of national authorities to recover unlawful state aid where national rules protecting the recipient of aid give rise to difficulties
THE COURT hereby rules

1. Community law requires the competent authority to revoke a decision granting unlawful aid, in accordance with a final decision of the Commission declaring the aid incompatible with the common market and ordering recovery, even if the authority has allowed the time-limit laid down for that purpose under national law in the interest of legal certainty to elapse.

2. Community law requires the competent authority to revoke a decision granting unlawful aid, in accordance with a final decision of the Commission declaring the aid incompatible with the common market and ordering recovery, even if the competent authority is responsible for the illegality of the aid decision to such a degree that revocation appears to be a breach of good faith towards the recipient, where the latter could not have had a legitimate expectation that the aid was lawful because the procedure laid down in article 93 of the Treaty had not been followed.

3. Community law requires the competent authority to revoke a decision granting unlawful aid, in accordance with a final decison of the Commission declaring the aid incompatible with the common market and ordering recovery, even where such recovery is excluded by national law because the gain no longer exists, in the absence of bad faith on the part of the recipient of the aid.
